extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of moral philosophy (readers of Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and interpretation of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (introduction and Book I–X excerpts), extracting the work's evaluative concepts such as practical/theoretical wisdom, happiness, pleasure, friendship, and teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two supreme forms of goodness of intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness of intellect has two supreme forms — Theoretical and Practical Wisdom. Theoretical apprehends the eternal laws of the universe and has no direct relation to human conduct; Practical Wisdom is identical with the master science of human life and supplies the right rules of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom formulates rules as they emerge from practical experience and organises them into a system converging upon happiness. Theoretical wisdom is about eternal truths; practical wisdom produces immediately applicable rules and can justify them by showing their connection to the end. Minor valuable forms include the power to think out policy in novel circumstances or to see the line of legal treatment to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical wisdom presupposes clear conception of the end and moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of producing practical rules presupposes (a) a clear and just apprehension of the nature of the end and the wish for it, and (b) a correct perception of the conditions of action; (a) is impossible except to a man whose character has been formed by discipline and who has acquired moral virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical wisdom and goodness of character are interdependent: neither is completely present without the other. Without moral virtue, practical 'wisdom' degenerates into merely worldly 'cleverness' — an unscrupulous parody of true practical wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true practical wisdom from 'cleverness' (unscrupulous competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Cleverness' is the parody of practical wisdom—wisdom of the unscrupulous man of the world that lacks goodness of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practical judgment not only for instrumental success but for its moral orientation and connection to virtuous character. Anti-pattern: praising rule-producing capacity that serves self-interest or immorally obtained ends as if it were phronesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for incontinence (weakness of will) by acknowledging reason in desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Incontinence (akrasia) is the phenomenon where a person knows the good yet chronically fails to act upon it; Aristotle locates its source in the nature of desire for bodily pleasures, which is not irrational but contains something rational and may mislead the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations of immoral action should not reduce failure to mere ignorance; they must recognise that passions can include reasons and that pleasures can be good within limits. The analysis must accommodate divided will and the rational elements within desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as necessary complement to moral theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Books VIII and IX treat friendship as an important and attractive complement to the more austere account of Greek morality in preceding books, containing profound reflections on the metaphysics of friendship or love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any full account of the moral life should incorporate friendship's role; treat friendship as more than incidental—as a necessary complement that affects character and well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity — 'the activity of a subject at its best acting upon an object at its best.' Pleasure is always a good but its value rises and falls with the worth of the activity it accompanies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pleasures by the quality of the activities they accompany. Highest pleasures are those that accompany the highest activities (e.g., intellectual contemplation). Avoid treating pleasure alone as the principal ingredient of the good life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness (chief good) identified with the contemplative life
rubrics_metrics.description: True Happiness cannot be found in practical life alone (moral virtues, civic life, military, or statesmanship) but rather in the life of the onlooker — the life of scientific and philosophic contemplation (the contemplative life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality of a life by the degree to which it allows intense intellectual activity and contemplation; other activities have value primarily insofar as they render contemplative life possible. Note Aristotle's emphasis on contemplation as intense, energising intellectual activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations/criticisms of the contemplative ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's presentation of the contemplative ideal has shortcomings: (1) its relation to the lower practical ideal is left obscure; (2) it appears realizable only by a gifted few and under exceptional circumstances; (3) its content seems unnecessarily and unjustifiably limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting or defending a contemplative account of the good, address these three criticisms: clarify relation to practice, consider accessibility, and justify the scope of goods included in the contemplative life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the State and law in promoting the best life
rubrics_metrics.description: The State, operating through Law (Reason backed by Force), is the great agency in producing the best life in the polis; ideally the best reason of the community should be embodied in its laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public legislation and education should aim to cultivate conditions that make the best life possible. Individuals who would make themselves and others better must study general principles of law, morality, and education — effectively becoming 'miniature legislators.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological view of human life and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human activity, especially practical activity, is directed towards a simple End discoverable by reflection; this End is conceived as the object of universal human desire and as something to be enjoyed. Aristotle's moral philosophy is eudaemonistic rather than hedonistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions in terms of their contribution toward an intelligible final end (Happiness). When analysing moral agents, foreground purposes and the nature of the end rather than merely formal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of actions derives from their efficiency as means to the end (prudential aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human practical activity derives its value from its efficiency as a means to the end; actions are good or bad, right or wrong, as they conduce or fail to conduce to Happiness. Right action presupposes Thought or Thinking (calculation of means to an end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actions by prudential standards of effectiveness toward the end, but be wary of reducing morality to mere instrumentalism; Aristotle himself notes the tendency to lower morality into a prosaic prudentialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral thinking should reveal the situation, not only calculate means
rubrics_metrics.description: The thinking which really matters in conduct is not merely imaginative forecasting or calculation of means; it is thinking which reveals to the agent the situation — both the universal situation and the ever-varying particular situation in which the individual finds himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral reasoning should combine knowledge of general principles with sensitivity to concrete, historical facts. The capacity to grasp the situation is central to freedom and to doing good; training should cultivate this perceptive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect generality rather than exactness in moral philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactness must not be looked for in all discussions alike; moral notions like nobleness and justice admit variation and error. From general data we should draw conclusions merely general and outline-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set appropriate methodological expectations: avoid demanding mathematical precision from moral philosophy. Present conclusions as general guides and be explicit about their conditionality and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate readiness for studying moral philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The young (in years or temperament) are not fit students of Moral Philosophy because they lack experience in actions of life and are apt to follow passions; knowledge is unprofitable for those of imperfect self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction is most profitable for those whose desires are formed and who can act in accordance with reason. Consider the maturity and character of learners when designing moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for an acceptable account of the Chief Good (Happiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good should be final (desired for its own sake), something that is one's own and not easily taken from one, and stable under misfortunes; common candidates (pleasure, wealth, honour) are inadequate because they are contingent or externally dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing a conception of happiness, test it against these requirements: finality, personal possession/stability, and resilience under adversity. Distinguish between lives of pleasure, honor (societal life), and contemplation when evaluating competing accounts.
